title: Talking Animals: the Serpent and Balaam's Donkey
lead: Two animals speak in the Bible's stories: the snake in Eden, who talks the woman into eating from the forbidden tree (Genesis 3:1–5), and Balaam's donkey, whose mouth the LORD opens to rebuke her master (Numbers 22:28–30). One speaks to deceive, the other to tell the truth a prophet could not see. Readers have taken them as miracles, as visions or as the language of story, and Christians from the New Testament on have seen the devil behind the snake (Revelation 12:9).

sections.b: "Now the snake was shrewder than every wild animal of the field that the LORD God had made" (Genesis 3:1). The Hebrew nachash is the ordinary word for a snake, and Genesis calls it one of the animals God made. There is a word play: the man and woman were 'arummim, "naked" (Genesis 2:25), and the snake was 'arum, "shrewd." The snake's first words twist what God said: "Is it really true that God said, 'You must not eat from any tree of the garden'?" (Genesis 3:1). After the fall God curses it to crawl on its belly (Genesis 3:14), and he adds: "He will strike you on the head, / and you will strike him on the heel" (Genesis 3:15). Genesis never names Satan, and readers differ on whether the snake is more than a snake. Josephus, retelling Genesis, makes the snake itself the tempter: in those days all the living creatures had one language, and God took the serpent's speech away as part of its punishment. He reads Genesis 3:15 as the reason people strike at a snake's head (Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 1). Other readers saw a spirit behind it. The Wisdom of Solomon (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, but not for Protestants or Jews) says that through the devil's envy death came into the world (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24). Revelation calls the dragon "the ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9), and Paul promises that "The God of peace will crush Satan under your feet" (Romans 16:20). Irenaeus read Genesis 3:15 as the first promise of Christ, the woman's offspring who would crush the serpent's head (Against Heresies 5.21.1).
sections.refs: Genesis 2:25; Genesis 3:1–5; Genesis 3:14–15; Revelation 12:9; Revelation 20:2; Romans 16:20; 2 Corinthians 11:3; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24

sections.b: Balaam rides out to curse Israel. Three times his donkey sees the angel of the LORD with a drawn sword and turns aside, and three times Balaam beats her. "Then the LORD opened the donkey's mouth" (Numbers 22:28), and she asks why. Only then does the LORD uncover Balaam's eyes (Numbers 22:31). The famous seer is blind, and his donkey sees; the angel tells him he would have been killed, "and her I would have kept alive" (Numbers 22:33). 2 Peter recalls the scene: "a voiceless beast of burden, speaking out in a human voice, stopped the prophet's madness" (2 Peter 2:16). The Mishnah lists "the mouth of the donkey" among ten things God made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath (Mishnah Avot 5:6), that is, a wonder planned from creation.

sections.h: How to read a speaking animal
sections.b: As a miracle in history. Many Jewish and Christian readers have taken both scenes as events. For the donkey, 2 Peter tells the scene as a rebuke that really happened (2 Peter 2:16), and the Mishnah counts "the mouth of the donkey" among the wonders made before the first Sabbath (Mishnah Avot 5:6). For the snake, readers who take the scene as an event differ on who spoke. Josephus has the snake speak for itself, out of envy (Jewish Antiquities, book 1, chapter 1). Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 13 says the fallen angel Sammael rode the serpent, and that it spoke only by Sammael's intention. Augustine wrote that the fallen angel "chose the serpent as his mouthpiece" (City of God 14.11). As a vision. Maimonides held that the speaking of Balaam's donkey happened in a prophetic vision, because an angel appears in the same account (Guide of the Perplexed 2:42). As a figure. Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of Jesus' day, said that taken at face value "a serpent uttering human speech" seems a marvel. Read for its hidden meaning, he said, the snake stands for pleasure (On Husbandry, section 22 in Richter's edition). The Bible itself can use talking trees in a fable without claiming that trees talk (Judges 9:8; 2 Kings 14:9), which shows that speaking creatures can belong to a kind of story. Whichever reading one takes, the two scenes make a matching point: speech belongs to God. The snake uses it to cast doubt on God's word. The donkey speaks only because "the LORD opened the donkey's mouth" (Numbers 22:28), and she speaks the truth.
